title: Brown Highlights Impact Fee Funding for Lawrence County Communities
raw_text:
Brown Highlights Impact Fee Funding for Lawrence County Communities
June 16, 2026
HARRISBURG - Rep. Marla Brown (R-Lawrence) today announced more than $612,000 in Marcellus Shale impact fee revenue is headed to communities throughout the 9th Legislative District and Lawrence County. Municipalities in the district will receive more than $308,000, while Lawrence County will receive more than $304,000 through the impact fee program.
“Impact fee revenue gives local officials the flexibility to address the unique needs of their communities,” said Brown. “Whether it's improving infrastructure, supporting public safety services or investing in future growth, these funds help ensure the benefits of Pennsylvania's energy production are felt here in Lawrence County.”
The following impact fee disbursements in the 9th District were announced:
•	Bessemer Borough - $1,611.
•	Hickory Township - $4,857.
•	Mahoning Township - $56,007.
•	Neshannock Township - $28,327.
•	New Castle City - $31,487.
•	New Wilmington Borough - $2,738.
•	North Beaver Township - $41,730.
•	Pulaski Township - $110,234.
•	S.N.P.J. Borough - $126.
•	Shenango Township - $13,603.
•	South New Castle Borough - $619.
•	Taylor Township - $2,292.
•	Union Township - $8,502.
•	Wilmington Township - $5,949.
For the reporting year of 2025, natural gas producers paid almost $244 million in impact fees statewide, bringing the total distributed through the program to more than $3.12 billion since its inception in 2012.
Under Act 13 of 2012, impact fees are collected from drilling companies, with a significant portion returned directly to counties and municipalities affected by natural gas development. The remaining revenue supports the Marcellus Shale Legacy Fund and statewide initiatives, including emergency response planning and training, water and sewer infrastructure improvements, environmental programs and transportation-related projects.
Representative Marla Brown
9th Legislative District
Pennsylvania House of Representatives

title: Brown Announces State Funding for Housing Rehabilitation and Community Revitalization Projects in Lawrence County
raw_text:
Brown Announces State Funding for Housing Rehabilitation and Community Revitalization Projects in Lawrence County
June 15, 2026
HARRISBURG - Rep. Marla Brown (R-Lawrence) today announced two Lawrence County projects have been awarded a total of $500,000 through the Pennsylvania Housing Affordability and Rehabilitation Enhancement (PHARE) program to support housing improvements, accessibility upgrades and community revitalization efforts.
The funding was approved this week by the Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency (PHFA) Board as part of a statewide investment in affordable housing and community development initiatives.
“Safe, affordable housing is essential to the strength and stability of our communities,” said Brown. “These investments will help improve housing conditions for seniors, individuals with disabilities and families throughout Lawrence County while also addressing blighted properties and supporting local economic development. I am pleased to see these resources coming back to our community to meet critical housing needs.”
The following projects were awarded funding:
•
Disability Options Network
- $200,000 for its Shelter Strong Lawrence County program. The initiative will help address the housing needs of seniors and individuals with disabilities by rehabilitating approximately 32 owner-occupied homes. Funding will provide up to $16,000 per home for low- and moderate-income residents to improve safety, accessibility and quality of life.
•
Lawrence County Department of Planning and Community Development
- $300,000 for its Countywide Housing Rehabilitation and Blight Removal Program. The project will support housing rehabilitation efforts, demolition of blighted structures and façade improvements for commercial buildings across Lawrence County.
The PHARE program is administered by the Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency and funded through two primary sources: a portion of the Marcellus Shale Impact Fee and Pennsylvania Realty Transfer Tax revenues. The program supports housing and community development initiatives designed to expand affordable housing opportunities and strengthen communities throughout the Commonwealth.
Statewide, PHFA approved more than $93 million in PHARE funding for 432 housing and community development initiatives across all 67 counties.
Representative Marla Brown
9th Legislative District
Pennsylvania House of Representatives

title: Brown Highlights Bipartisan Record on Data Center Oversight
raw_text:
Brown Highlights Bipartisan Record on Data Center Oversight
June 2, 2026
HARRISBURG – Rep. Marla Brown (R-Lawrence) released the following statement regarding her stance on data center development in Pennsylvania:
“As Pennsylvania continues to attract interest from data center developers, it is important that we balance economic opportunity with responsible oversight. With increasing demand for artificial intelligence, Pennsylvania is seeing a growing interest from developers looking to build large-scale data centers across the Commonwealth.
“My record shows I have supported bipartisan efforts to increase transparency, strengthen oversight and give local communities a greater voice. I voted in favor of two Democrat-sponsored bills addressing data center development because I believe good policy should always come before politics.
“I voted for
House Bill 2150
, which would require data centers to report their energy and water usage, and
House Bill 2151
, which would direct the state to develop model zoning guidance to help municipalities address future development. Both bills were sponsored by Democratic lawmakers and received bipartisan support.
“I also introduced
House Bill 2588
, which would prohibit data centers from being built on prime farmland that is currently in active agricultural use. The legislation is designed to preserve Pennsylvania’s most productive agricultural land while allowing data center development to continue in more appropriate locations.
“Data centers can bring investment, construction jobs and long-term economic growth to Pennsylvania. At the same time, municipalities need clear guidance and sufficient time to evaluate how these large-scale projects may impact local infrastructure, land use, water resources and energy demand.
“It is also important the costs associated with serving these facilities do not fall on homeowners, seniors and small businesses through higher utility bills. Large-scale developments should be planned responsibly, with transparency, local input, and protections for ratepayers.
“I will continue supporting policies that encourage investment and innovation while ensuring local communities have a voice, local governments have the tools they need, and Pennsylvania families are protected.”
Representative Marla Brown
9th Legislative District
Pennsylvania House of Representatives

Brown: Budget Misses the Mark on Fiscal Responsibility
raw_text:
Brown: Budget Misses the Mark on Fiscal Responsibility
July 12, 2026
HARRISBURG
– Rep. Marla Brown (R-Lawrence), a member of the House Appropriations Committee, voted against the General Appropriations bill for the 2026-27 fiscal year. The measure passed the House and now heads to Gov. Josh Shapiro for his signature. Brown issued the following statement:
“Voting on the state budget is one of the General Assembly’s most important responsibilities. At a time when families across Lawrence County are struggling with the rising cost of living, we should be focused on controlling government spending and protecting taxpayers. While this budget includes several worthwhile investments, I could not support the final package because it relies on unsustainable spending practices and accounting maneuvers that fail to provide taxpayers with a clear picture of the Commonwealth’s financial future.
“One of my biggest concerns is Medicaid payment cycle shifts make it more difficult for taxpayers to see the true cost of government spending. While this budget is being presented as a $50.8 billion spending plan, those shifts bring the total spending closer to $52 billion. That is not the level of transparency Pennsylvanians deserve. I am also concerned this budget nearly exhausts the state’s available reserve funds while failing to address the Commonwealth’s growing structural imbalance. We cannot continue relying on short-term solutions and expect future taxpayers to absorb the cost.
“We also need to prioritize policies that generate sustainable, long-term revenue growth. That includes meaningful permit reform to reduce unnecessary delays and make it easier for businesses to invest and create jobs. Instead of relying on accounting maneuvers and one-time budget fixes, we should be growing our economy by attracting new employers and expanding our tax base.
“However, I was pleased to see several priorities included in the budget. The $10 million investment in career and technical education will help prepare students for rewarding careers in high-demand fields, and funding for the Rapid Bridge and Road Deployment Program will help improve critical infrastructure across the Commonwealth. I am pleased this budget does not include combined reporting or the legalization of recreational marijuana.
“My constituents expect us to make responsible decisions with their tax dollars. We can invest in priorities such as education, infrastructure and workforce development while also controlling spending and protecting taxpayers. Unfortunately, this budget does not strike that balance, which is why I voted no.”
Representative Marla Brown
9th Legislative District
Pennsylvania House of Representatives

Brown: Budget Misses the Mark on Fiscal Responsibility
July 12, 2026
HARRISBURG
– Rep. Marla Brown (R-Lawrence), a member of the House Appropriations Committee, voted against the General Appropriations bill for the 2026-27 fiscal year. The measure passed the House and now heads to Gov. Josh Shapiro for his signature. Brown issued the following statement:
“Voting on the state budget is one of the General Assembly’s most important responsibilities. At a time when families across Lawrence County are struggling with the rising cost of living, we should be focused on controlling government spending and protecting taxpayers. While this budget includes several worthwhile investments, I could not support the final package because it relies on unsustainable spending practices and accounting maneuvers that fail to provide taxpayers with a clear picture of the Commonwealth’s financial future.
“One of my biggest concerns is Medicaid payment cycle shifts make it more difficult for taxpayers to see the true cost of government spending. While this budget is being presented as a $50.8 billion spending plan, those shifts bring the total spending closer to $52 billion. That is not the level of transparency Pennsylvanians deserve. I am also concerned this budget nearly exhausts the state’s available reserve funds while failing to address the Commonwealth’s growing structural imbalance. We cannot continue relying on short-term solutions and expect future taxpayers to absorb the cost.
“We also need to prioritize policies that generate sustainable, long-term revenue growth. That includes meaningful permit reform to reduce unnecessary delays and make it easier for businesses to invest and create jobs. Instead of relying on accounting maneuvers and one-time budget fixes, we should be growing our economy by attracting new employers and expanding our tax base.
“However, I was pleased to see several priorities included in the budget. The $10 million investment in career and technical education will help prepare students for rewarding careers in high-demand fields, and funding for the Rapid Bridge and Road Deployment Program will help improve critical infrastructure across the Commonwealth. I am pleased this budget does not include combined reporting or the legalization of recreational marijuana.
“My constituents expect us to make responsible decisions with their tax dollars. We can invest in priorities such as education, infrastructure and workforce development while also controlling spending and protecting taxpayers. Unfortunately, this budget does not strike that balance, which is why I voted no.”
Representative Marla Brown
9th Legislative District
Pennsylvania House of Representatives

title: Brown Announces Farmland Preservation in Lawrence County
raw_text:
Brown Announces Farmland Preservation in Lawrence County
October 9, 2026
HARRISBURG
– Rep. Marla Brown (R-Lawrence) announced today a 72-acre livestock farm in Pulaski Township will be preserved through Pennsylvania’s Farmland Preservation Program, protecting the property from future residential or commercial development.
The farm, owned by Mitchell James and Cassidy Noelle Whiting, is among 22 farms across 14 counties recently approved for preservation by the State Agriculture Land Preservation Board. The latest round of approvals protects a total of 1,228 acres of Pennsylvania farmland.
“Preserving farmland helps protect our agricultural heritage, support our farming communities and ensure future generations can continue producing the food and resources we depend on,” said Brown. “Protecting this 72-acre farm in Lawrence County is an investment in our local community and helps keep valuable agricultural land available for farming rather than future development.”
Through the Farmland Preservation Program, development rights are purchased from willing landowners to ensure preserved properties remain dedicated to agricultural use and are protected from future residential or commercial development.
With the latest approvals, Pennsylvania’s Farmland Preservation Program has protected 6,781 farms totaling 671,082 acres across 58 counties. Since the program began in 1988, more than $1.83 billion in state, county and local funds has been invested to preserve farmland throughout the Commonwealth.

title: Brown Announces State Grants for Lawrence County Community Projects
raw_text:
Brown Announces State Grants for Lawrence County Community Projects
September 15, 2026
LAWRENCE COUNTY - Rep. Marla Brown (R-Lawrence) today announced more than $1.1 million in Local Share Account (LSA) grants have been approved by the Commonwealth Financing Authority (CFA) to support economic development, wastewater infrastructure, public safety communications and other critical community improvements across Lawrence County.
Local Share Account grants are funded through gaming revenues under Act 71 of 2004 and are used to support economic development, community improvement and other projects that enhance the quality of life for Pennsylvania residents.
“These projects represent the kind of investments that help Lawrence County move forward,” said Brown. “I’m proud to see state funding coming back to our communities to address long-standing needs and help position Lawrence County for continued growth and success.”
The approved Lawrence County projects include:
•
Lawrence County Economic Development Corporation - $200,000
to redevelop the former R.E. Whittaker Roto Wash facility in New Castle City into an industrial site. The project will demolish approximately 19,000 square feet of deteriorated structures and construct a new 10,500-square-foot leasable industrial building, along with site utilities, stormwater improvements, parking and lighting. The site is expected to support approximately 10-15 businesses. LSA funds will be used for construction costs.
•
Mahoning Township - $350,000
to upgrade equipment at the township’s wastewater treatment plant and pump stations. Improvements include installation of a Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) system, replacement of the wastewater treatment plant centrifuge, pump station duplex pumps and two speed reducers. The upgrades will improve monitoring, efficiency and reliability while reducing breakdowns and long-term operating and maintenance costs. LSA funds will be used for construction, equipment purchase and installation, and engineering costs.
•
New Wilmington Borough - $114,267
to purchase new radios for the borough’s police department. The project includes eight portable radios, four mobile units for police vehicles, a base radio unit and a multi-band antenna to replace outdated equipment that is no longer supported by the manufacturer and cannot communicate with local college and neighboring county systems. LSA funds will be used for the purchase and installation of equipment.
•
North Beaver Township Municipal Authority - $200,000
to construct new grinder pumps as part of an effort to address aging sewer infrastructure. The project will help prevent residential sewer backups, protect the environment and safeguard treatment facility equipment while providing a cost-effective, low-maintenance solution for challenging wastewater conditions. LSA funds will be used for site preparation, infrastructure and engineering costs.
•
Taylor Township - $250,000
to upgrade the township’s sewage treatment plant. The project will address the age of the existing facility, improve solids handling, increase treatment capacity and resolve site-related issues through improvements outlined in the township’s updated Act 537 Plan. LSA funds will be used for infrastructure costs.
The Commonwealth Financing Authority is an independent agency responsible for administering state investments that promote economic growth, infrastructure development and community revitalization throughout Pennsylvania.

title: Brown, Bernstine Announce State Funding for Local Historical Societies
raw_text:
Brown, Bernstine Announce State Funding for Local Historical Societies
September 11, 2026
LAWRENCE/BUTLER COUNTIES
- Reps. Marla Brown (R-Lawrence) and Aaron Bernstine (R-Butler/Lawrence) today announced state funding totaling $19,000 for historical organizations in Lawrence and Butler counties through the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission’s Cultural and Historical Support Grant Program.
“The Lawrence County Historical Society plays an important role in preserving the stories, records and artifacts that tell the history of our communities,” said Brown. “This funding will help the society continue that work and ensure these valuable pieces of our past remain available for residents and future generations.”
“Preserving our history takes the resources to properly care for them,” said Bernstine. “I’m pleased to see this funding support both the Butler and Lawrence County historical societies and the important work they do to protect our local heritage.”
The Lawrence County Historical Society will receive a $9,500 grant. The funding will help offset operating expenses, including utilities, needed to maintain proper temperature and humidity levels for the society’s extensive collection of historical records and artifacts. The funding also will help provide a comfortable working environment for volunteers.
The society collects, preserves and displays artifacts related to the county’s heritage. It maintains a 1905 historical home and museum, an office building and extensive collections of books; family histories; cemetery records; and business, school and church histories. The society also hosts historical and community events throughout the year.
The Butler County Historical Society will receive a $9,500 grant. The funding will support the repair and maintenance of the society’s three early 19th-century properties, as well as the purchase of supplies and equipment for collections management and salary expenses for its collections manager.
The society collects, catalogs, archives and preserves objects, documents and images relating to Butler County’s history and heritage. Through tours, events, field trips and educational programs, the society makes its collections and historic buildings accessible to residents and visitors.
The Cultural and Historical Support Grant Program provides general operating support to museums and official county historical societies across Pennsylvania.

title: Brown: Data Center Development Must Respect Our Communities
raw_text:
Brown: Data Center Development Must Respect Our Communities
August 20, 2026
HARRISBURG
- Rep. Marla Brown (R-Lawrence) issued the following statement after Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order restricting data center development:
“My position on data centers has been clear and consistent from the start. Unfortunately, the governor has not shared that position. It appears he has finally seen the light and recognized the need for greater oversight of these massive projects.
“Pennsylvania needs economic investment and new opportunities, but that growth must come with reasonable boundaries and protections for our communities.
“There is no place for massive data centers in residential neighborhoods or on farmland. I have authored, supported and voted for legislation that reflects this position, while also working with our townships and county officials to ensure they have the support and tools they need to protect their communities.
“We need transparency, strong environmental protections and accountability. Data centers should pay their fair share, and Pennsylvania families and small businesses should never be left paying the bill for these massive projects.
“But above all, local control matters. The people who live in these communities deserve a voice in what is built in their backyards. Economic development should work for Pennsylvania families, not come at their expense.”
Representative Marla Brown

“But above all, local control matters. The people who live in these communities deserve a voice in what is built in their backyards. Economic development should work for Pennsylvania families, not come at their expense.”

August 13, 2026
HARRISBURG
- Rep. Marla Brown (R-Lawrence) today announced two agricultural businesses in the 9th Legislative District have been awarded a combined $171,920 through the second round of Pennsylvania’s Agricultural Innovation Grant Program.
The grants will help local agricultural businesses invest in innovative technology designed to improve efficiency, productivity and profitability while supporting the long-term sustainability of Pennsylvania agriculture.
The Lawrence County recipients are:
•
Dawson’s Orchards - $42,120
- Funding for an automated grading system for orchard crops.
•
Den-Be Farms - $129,800
- Funding for a robotic milking system.
“These grants are a great example of how investing in innovation can help our local agricultural businesses become more efficient, productive and competitive,” said Brown. “Our farmers and agricultural businesses work hard every day to produce the food we depend on, and they deserve access to the tools and technology that can help them succeed. I am looking forward to seeing the results of these investments in the years ahead.”
The Agricultural Innovation Grant Program is designed to help farmers and other agricultural businesses adopt new technologies, conservation practices and renewable-energy solutions. Grants can support projects that improve farm or processing efficiency, enhance production, protect soil and water resources, reduce waste, improve energy use, and implement innovative tools for managing crops, livestock and agricultural operations.

title: Brown: Budget Misses the Mark on Fiscal Responsibility
raw_text:
Brown: Budget Misses the Mark on Fiscal Responsibility
July 12, 2026
HARRISBURG
– Rep. Marla Brown (R-Lawrence), a member of the House Appropriations Committee, voted against the General Appropriations bill for the 2026-27 fiscal year. The measure passed the House and now heads to Gov. Josh Shapiro for his signature. Brown issued the following statement:
“Voting on the state budget is one of the General Assembly’s most important responsibilities. At a time when families across Lawrence County are struggling with the rising cost of living, we should be focused on controlling government spending and protecting taxpayers. While this budget includes several worthwhile investments, I could not support the final package because it relies on unsustainable spending practices and accounting maneuvers that fail to provide taxpayers with a clear picture of the Commonwealth’s financial future.
“One of my biggest concerns is Medicaid payment cycle shifts make it more difficult for taxpayers to see the true cost of government spending. While this budget is being presented as a $50.8 billion spending plan, those shifts bring the total spending closer to $52 billion. That is not the level of transparency Pennsylvanians deserve. I am also concerned this budget nearly exhausts the state’s available reserve funds while failing to address the Commonwealth’s growing structural imbalance. We cannot continue relying on short-term solutions and expect future taxpayers to absorb the cost.
“We also need to prioritize policies that generate sustainable, long-term revenue growth. That includes meaningful permit reform to reduce unnecessary delays and make it easier for businesses to invest and create jobs. Instead of relying on accounting maneuvers and one-time budget fixes, we should be growing our economy by attracting new employers and expanding our tax base.
“However, I was pleased to see several priorities included in the budget. The $10 million investment in career and technical education will help prepare students for rewarding careers in high-demand fields, and funding for the Rapid Bridge and Road Deployment Program will help improve critical infrastructure across the Commonwealth. I am pleased this budget does not include combined reporting or the legalization of recreational marijuana.
“My constituents expect us to make responsible decisions with their tax dollars. We can invest in priorities such as education, infrastructure and workforce development while also controlling spending and protecting taxpayers. Unfortunately, this budget does not strike that balance, which is why I voted no.”
Representative Marla Brown
9th Legislative District
Pennsylvania House of Representatives

title: Brown Highlights Impact Fee Funding for Lawrence County Communities
raw_text:
Brown Highlights Impact Fee Funding for Lawrence County Communities
June 16, 2026
HARRISBURG - Rep. Marla Brown (R-Lawrence) today announced more than $612,000 in Marcellus Shale impact fee revenue is headed to communities throughout the 9th Legislative District and Lawrence County. Municipalities in the district will receive more than $308,000, while Lawrence County will receive more than $304,000 through the impact fee program.
“Impact fee revenue gives local officials the flexibility to address the unique needs of their communities,” said Brown. “Whether it's improving infrastructure, supporting public safety services or investing in future growth, these funds help ensure the benefits of Pennsylvania's energy production are felt here in Lawrence County.”
The following impact fee disbursements in the 9th District were announced:
•	Bessemer Borough - $1,611.
•	Hickory Township - $4,857.
•	Mahoning Township - $56,007.
•	Neshannock Township - $28,327.
•	New Castle City - $31,487.
•	New Wilmington Borough - $2,738.
•	North Beaver Township - $41,730.
•	Pulaski Township - $110,234.
•	S.N.P.J. Borough - $126.
•	Shenango Township - $13,603.
•	South New Castle Borough - $619.
•	Taylor Township - $2,292.
•	Union Township - $8,502.
•	Wilmington Township - $5,949.
For the reporting year of 2025, natural gas producers paid almost $244 million in impact fees statewide, bringing the total distributed through the program to more than $3.12 billion since its inception in 2012.
Under Act 13 of 2012, impact fees are collected from drilling companies, with a significant portion returned directly to counties and municipalities affected by natural gas development. The remaining revenue supports the Marcellus Shale Legacy Fund and statewide initiatives, including emergency response planning and training, water and sewer infrastructure improvements, environmental programs and transportation-related projects.
Representative Marla Brown
9th Legislative District
Pennsylvania House of Representatives
